Immediately following mining the water table will be near the base of the spoil material in the excavation but should rise with time. The steady state of the equilibrium ground-water surface will be a function of the recharge, discharge, and permeability of the reclaimed aquifer. Recharge will include lateral ground-water inflow from the south through bedrock (including coal) on Tract III and the infiltration from precipitation on both tracts. The rate of infiltration will probably be higher after reclamation than under natural conditions because of increased permeability, except in areas which before mining had clinker at the surface.
In general, mining will steepen hydraulic gradients on the south part of Tract III and diminish or flatten gradients on the north part of Tract III. There will be some increased lateral flow initially into the mine and reclaimed areas from the unmined areas adjacent to the southern part of Tract III. On the southwest side of Tract III, the Middle Fork of Sarpy Creek is expected to benefit by increased spring discharge. This discharge will occur at the contact of the bottom of the reclaimed aquifer with the top of the sub-Robinson unit where it crops out in the stream valley. Because the water table within the reclaimed aquifer is expected to be in a low position, essentially no spring discharge will occur to shallow drainageways upon the reclaimed surface in interior areas.
